questions.stem: RESPA was enacted primarily to:
options: Set maximum interest rates on mortgages
Guarantee loan approval for first-time buyers
Require disclosure of settlement costs and prohibit abusive practices like kickbacks
questions.explanation: RESPA's core purposes are to give consumers clear disclosure of settlement (closing) costs and to eliminate abusive practices such as kickbacks and referral fees that inflate those costs. It does not cap interest rates, guarantee approval, or set monetary policy.

questions.stem: Under RESPA, a 'mortgage broker' is generally:
options: A person who brings a borrower and lender together but does not fund the loan
questions.explanation: A mortgage broker arranges or negotiates a loan between borrower and lender for compensation but typically does not use its own funds to make the loan. RESPA governs its fees and referral arrangements.

questions.stem: Which loan is generally covered by RESPA?
options: A federally related mortgage loan on a 1-4 family residential property
An unsecured personal line of credit
A business loan to a corporation
A loan secured by a 25-acre commercial farm
questions.explanation: RESPA applies to federally related mortgage loans secured by a first or subordinate lien on 1-4 family residential property. Business-purpose loans, commercial/agricultural loans over the acreage thresholds, and unsecured credit fall outside its scope.

questions.stem: A settlement agent offers an MLO $250 for each closed loan the MLO refers, with no service performed in exchange. Under RESPA, this arrangement is:
options: A prohibited referral fee subject to criminal penalties
Permissible if the borrower is told about it in writing
Permissible because settlement services are involved
Permissible if the payment stays under $500 per loan
questions.explanation: RESPA Section 8(a) prohibits giving or accepting any fee, kickback, or thing of value for referring settlement-service business. A payment tied purely to referrals, with no compensable service rendered, is exactly the conduct banned, and it carries criminal exposure (fines up to $10,000 and up to one year in prison). Disclosure to the borrower does not cure a Section 8 violation, the presence of settlement services does not make a referral fee legal, and there is no dollar-amount safe harbor that permits it.

questions.stem: An MLO wants to require borrowers to use a specific title company the MLO owns. Under RESPA this is:
options: Prohibited as required use, absent limited exceptions and proper ABA disclosure
questions.explanation: RESPA generally bars requiring the use of a particular provider ('required use'). Referrals to an affiliate are allowed only with an Affiliated Business Arrangement disclosure and without requiring use, except for limited attorney/title exceptions.

questions.stem: Charging a borrower a fee for preparing the Closing Disclosure or TILA disclosures is:
options: Prohibited; a lender may not charge a fee specifically for preparing required disclosures
questions.explanation: RESPA prohibits charging a fee specifically for preparing the statutorily required disclosures (Closing Disclosure, escrow statements, TILA disclosures). Legitimate origination fees for services are separate.

questions.stem: Under RESPA, a 'settlement service' includes:
options: Title searches, attorney services, and loan origination
The real estate agent's car payment
questions.explanation: Settlement services are services provided in connection with a real estate settlement, such as title searches and insurance, attorney services, document preparation, appraisals, and loan origination. Unrelated personal expenses are not settlement services.

questions.stem: Under Regulation X, information collected on a mortgage application is used to:
options: Evaluate the borrower and produce required disclosures
questions.explanation: Application information supports evaluating the borrower and generating required disclosures (Loan Estimate, etc.). RESPA/Reg X governs the settlement-cost disclosures that flow from the application.

questions.stem: Under RESPA servicing rules, before making the first foreclosure filing a servicer generally must:
options: Wait until the borrower is more than 120 days delinquent
File immediately upon one missed payment
questions.explanation: RESPA generally prohibits a servicer from making the first notice or filing for foreclosure until the borrower is more than 120 days delinquent, giving time to pursue loss-mitigation options.

questions.stem: RESPA requires a servicer to provide an initial escrow account statement:
options: Only if the borrower requests it
Every month with the payment coupon
At settlement or within 45 days of establishing the escrow account
Only when the loan is paid off
questions.explanation: The initial escrow account statement must be delivered at settlement or within 45 days of establishing the escrow account. It itemizes estimated taxes, insurance, and other charges to be paid from escrow. Annual statements follow thereafter.

questions.stem: An annual escrow analysis reveals a shortage. RESPA generally allows the servicer to:
options: Demand full repayment immediately with no options
Offer the borrower the option to repay the shortage over at least 12 months (for smaller shortages)
questions.explanation: For an escrow shortage, RESPA generally requires the servicer to allow repayment of smaller shortages over a period of at least 12 months, rather than demanding an immediate lump sum.

questions.stem: Under ECOA, a creditor MAY ask about an applicant's:
options: National origin, to deny the loan
Obligation to pay alimony or child support that the applicant relies on for repayment
questions.explanation: A creditor may ask about alimony/child support if the applicant chooses to rely on it for qualifying, and must consider it. Inquiries into religion, childbearing intentions, or using national origin to deny are prohibited.

questions.stem: An applicant qualifies for a loan on their own. Under ECOA, the creditor:
options: May require the applicant's parent to co-sign
Must require a co-signer for all married applicants
May not require a co-signer if the applicant independently qualifies
May require a spouse to co-sign anyway
questions.explanation: If an applicant qualifies on their own under the creditor's standards, ECOA prohibits requiring a co-signer, and a creditor may not require that the co-signer be the applicant's spouse if a co-signer is legitimately needed. Requiring a spouse's signature when not necessary is a violation.

questions.stem: Under ECOA, part-time income the applicant relies on:
options: Must be considered and may not be discounted solely because it is part-time
questions.explanation: A creditor may not automatically discount or exclude income because it is part-time, from public assistance, or from protected sources; it must be considered to the extent it is likely to continue.

questions.stem: Which factor is a legitimate creditworthiness consideration under ECOA?
options: Marital status in a non-community-property context
The applicant's credit history and payment record
questions.explanation: Credit history and payment record are legitimate. ECOA prohibits reliance on religion, childbearing, and (except in limited community-property situations) marital status.

questions.stem: Which is a prohibited basis for discrimination under ECOA?
questions.explanation: ECOA prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, or because income comes from public assistance. DTI, credit score, and LTV are legitimate creditworthiness factors a creditor may weigh.

questions.stem: Which is a permissible reason to deny a mortgage application under ECOA?
options: Insufficient income to support the requested payment
questions.explanation: Denials must rest on legitimate creditworthiness factors such as insufficient income, excessive DTI, or poor credit. Marital status, receipt of protected income, and national origin are prohibited bases.

questions.stem: Regulation B implements which federal law?
questions.explanation: Regulation B implements the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA). Reg X = RESPA, Reg Z = TILA, Reg C = HMDA.

questions.stem: ECOA requires notification of action taken on a completed application within:
questions.explanation: A creditor must notify the applicant of action taken (approval, counteroffer, adverse action, or incompleteness) within 30 days of receiving a completed application.

questions.stem: An ECOA adverse action notice must include:
options: The names of other applicants who were approved
The specific reasons for the action or how to request them, and the ECOA notice
questions.explanation: An adverse action notice must state the specific principal reasons for the action (or disclose the right to request them) and include the ECOA anti-discrimination notice and the credit bureau's contact information when a report was used. It does not disclose other applicants' data or the creditor's financials.

questions.stem: Under ECOA, notice of adverse action on a completed application must be provided within:
questions.explanation: ECOA and Regulation B require notice of adverse action within 30 days after receiving a completed application. The same 30-day framework governs notices of approval, counteroffers, and incompleteness. The three-business-day option borrows from TILA disclosure timing; 15 and 60 days are not the ECOA standard.

questions.stem: Which is an 'adverse action' requiring an ECOA notice?
options: Approving the loan as applied for
questions.explanation: Adverse action includes a denial or a revocation of credit, or an unfavorable change in terms. Approval as requested and an accepted counteroffer are not adverse action; a denial is.

questions.stem: When adverse action is based on a credit score, the notice must include:
options: The credit score, range, and key factors that adversely affected it
questions.explanation: If a credit score was used in taking adverse action, the FCRA requires the notice to include the score, the range of possible scores, and the key factors that adversely affected it, along with the credit bureau's details.

questions.stem: Under ECOA/Regulation B, an applicant is considered 'elderly' if they are:
questions.explanation: Regulation B defines 'elderly' as age 62 or older. Age generally may not be used against an applicant, though a creditor may consider it favorably (for example, treating an applicant's advanced age as a positive factor) under the empirically derived, demonstrably sound rules.

questions.stem: A borrower declines to provide the ethnicity, sex, and race information in Section 8 of the URLA during a face-to-face application. The MLO should:
options: Note that the borrower declined and record the information by visual observation or surname as required
Enter assumptions and treat them as borrower-supplied facts
Refuse to continue until the borrower answers
Leave the application incomplete and stop working on it
questions.explanation: Section 8 demographic data supports HMDA and fair-lending monitoring. Borrowers may decline, but for applications taken in person the MLO must still note the information on the basis of visual observation or surname. The MLO never refuses the application over this, never treats it as a stopping point, and never records assumptions as if the borrower supplied them.
questions.primary_source_citation: Regulation C, 12 CFR §1003.4(a)(10); Appendix B to Part 1003

questions.stem: For a face-to-face application where the borrower declines to provide demographic information, the MLO must:
options: Guess and record it as borrower-provided
Note the information based on visual observation or surname
questions.explanation: Government monitoring information supports fair-lending oversight. If the applicant declines during an in-person application, the MLO must note ethnicity, race, and sex based on visual observation or surname, and mark that the applicant declined.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of TILA is to:
options: Promote informed use of credit through disclosure of terms and cost (APR, finance charge)
questions.explanation: TILA promotes the informed use of consumer credit by requiring meaningful disclosure of credit terms, most importantly the finance charge and the annual percentage rate (APR), so consumers can compare offers. It does not guarantee rates, insure loans, or handle licensing.

questions.stem: TILA generally applies to a loan that is:
options: A business loan to an LLC
Consumer credit secured by a dwelling
questions.explanation: TILA applies to consumer credit, including consumer loans secured by a dwelling. Business, commercial, and agricultural credit are generally exempt.

questions.stem: How does the APR differ from the note (interest) rate?
options: The APR reflects the interest rate plus certain finance charges, so it is usually higher
The note rate includes closing costs; the APR does not
questions.explanation: The note rate is the periodic interest charged on the balance. The APR expresses the cost of credit as a yearly rate that also folds in certain prepaid finance charges (points, some fees), so it is typically higher than the note rate. This lets borrowers compare total credit cost.

questions.stem: Under TILA, the 'finance charge' is:
options: The cost of consumer credit as a dollar amount, including interest and certain fees
questions.explanation: The finance charge is the total dollar cost of credit to the consumer, including interest and certain fees imposed as a condition of the loan. It feeds the APR calculation.

questions.stem: Under TILA, the 'amount financed' is:
options: The loan amount provided to the borrower, less prepaid finance charges
questions.explanation: The amount financed is the credit extended to the borrower, calculated as the principal minus prepaid finance charges. It differs from the total of payments, which includes all interest over the term.

questions.stem: A consumer closes on a loan to purchase their primary residence and, two days later, wants to cancel under the right of rescission. What is the correct response?
options: They may cancel within three years
They may cancel only if the appraisal was late
The right of rescission does not apply to a purchase-money loan
They may cancel by the end of the third business day
questions.explanation: The TILA right of rescission does not extend to residential mortgage (purchase-money) transactions secured by the consumer's principal dwelling. It applies to refinances with a new creditor, home-equity lines, and home-improvement loans on the principal dwelling. Because this is a purchase, there is no three-business-day or three-year rescission right, and the appraisal timing is irrelevant to whether rescission applies.

questions.stem: On a refinance of a principal residence with a new creditor, the lender never delivered the notice of the right to rescind. How long may the consumer have to rescind?
options: Thirty days from the first payment
Three business days from consummation, regardless
There is no rescission right on a refinance
Up to three years, because required notice/disclosures were not provided
questions.explanation: When the lender fails to deliver the notice of the right to rescind or the material TILA disclosures, the rescission window extends from three business days to as long as three years. The three-business-day period assumes proper delivery, so it does not control here. The thirty-day option is a distractor drawn from ECOA timing, and a new-creditor refinance of a principal dwelling is in fact rescindable.

questions.stem: For a rescindable loan, the creditor must give each consumer with the right to rescind:
options: Two copies of the notice of the right to rescind
questions.explanation: Each consumer entitled to rescind must receive two copies of the written notice of the right to rescind (one to keep, one to exercise the right), plus the material disclosures.

questions.stem: A borrower validly rescinds a refinance. Within how long must the creditor return money and release its security interest?
questions.explanation: After a valid rescission, the creditor generally has 20 calendar days to return any money or property and reflect that the security interest is void. The borrower then tenders back loan proceeds.

questions.stem: A loan is classified as a high-cost mortgage under HOEPA. Which is restricted or prohibited?
options: Balloon payments and most prepayment penalties
questions.explanation: HOEPA adds protections to high-cost mortgages: it restricts balloon payments, prohibits most prepayment penalties, bans loan-flipping and steering, and requires homeownership counseling before the loan. Income verification and disclosures remain required.

questions.stem: For a higher-priced mortgage loan (HPML) secured by a first lien on a principal dwelling, the creditor generally must:
options: Establish an escrow account for taxes and insurance for a minimum period
questions.explanation: HPML rules generally require the creditor to establish an escrow account for property taxes and insurance for at least the first five years on a first-lien principal-dwelling HPML, with limited exemptions (e.g., certain small creditors). They also trigger additional appraisal requirements.

questions.stem: For a higher-priced mortgage loan, the appraisal rules generally require:
options: A written appraisal with a physical interior inspection by a licensed appraiser
questions.explanation: HPML rules require a written appraisal based on a physical, interior property inspection by a certified or licensed appraiser, with a free copy to the borrower, and a second appraisal in certain flipping situations.

questions.stem: Under the Loan Originator Compensation rule, an MLO's compensation may NOT be based on:
options: A fixed percentage of the loan amount, set in advance
A loan's interest rate or other transaction terms
questions.explanation: Reg Z prohibits compensating an originator based on the terms of a transaction (such as the interest rate). Compensation may be based on loan amount, a fixed per-loan amount, or hourly/salary, but tying pay to rate or terms incentivizes steering and is barred. Dual compensation (from both consumer and another party) is also prohibited.

questions.stem: The TRID rule integrated disclosures from which two laws?
questions.explanation: TRID (TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure) combined the former GFE and initial TIL into the Loan Estimate, and the HUD-1 and final TIL into the Closing Disclosure, integrating RESPA and TILA disclosure requirements into two consumer forms.

questions.stem: Upon a consumer's request, a creditor must generally provide:
options: The specific reasons a particular charge or term was set, per applicable rules
questions.explanation: Consumers are entitled to certain information on request, such as the basis for adverse action reasons (ECOA) and copies of appraisals/valuations (ECOA valuations rule). Creditors must respond as the applicable rule requires.

questions.stem: A refinance with the SAME creditor on a principal dwelling is rescindable:
options: Only to the extent new money exceeds the existing balance plus refinance costs
questions.explanation: When refinancing with the same creditor, rescission generally applies only to the 'new money' portion, the amount financed that exceeds the unpaid balance, earned finance charges, and refinancing costs, not the entire loan.

questions.stem: The annual escrow account statement provided to a borrower shows:
options: Account activity and projected escrow payments for the coming year
questions.explanation: The annual escrow statement summarizes the prior year's escrow activity and projects the coming year's escrow payments and any surplus or shortage. It helps the borrower understand payment changes driven by taxes and insurance.

questions.stem: TRID's Loan Estimate/Closing Disclosure requirements generally apply to:
options: Most closed-end consumer mortgages secured by real property
questions.explanation: TRID applies to most closed-end consumer credit transactions secured by real property. HELOCs, reverse mortgages, and certain other loans use different disclosures and are excluded.

questions.stem: The Loan Estimate discloses all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Estimated closing costs and cash to close
Estimated interest rate and monthly payment
questions.explanation: The Loan Estimate discloses the rate, payment, closing costs, cash to close, and features like whether the rate or balance can increase. It does not print the borrower's credit score.

questions.stem: For TRID purposes, 'consummation' occurs when:
options: The consumer becomes contractually obligated on the loan
The borrower's offer is accepted by the seller
questions.explanation: Consummation is the time a consumer becomes contractually obligated on the credit transaction (determined by state law), which is not necessarily the same day as closing/settlement. The Closing Disclosure must be received at least three business days before consummation.

questions.stem: The special information booklet (home-buying/settlement-cost booklet) must generally be provided:
options: Within three business days of receiving an application for a purchase loan
questions.explanation: For most purchase-money transactions, the creditor must deliver the special information booklet within three business days of receiving the application. It is generally not required for refinances or certain other transactions.

questions.stem: The Closing Disclosure differs from the Loan Estimate in that it shows:
options: The actual, final loan terms and closing costs
questions.explanation: The Closing Disclosure presents the final, actual terms and costs, allowing the borrower to compare against the earlier Loan Estimate. It must be received at least three business days before consummation.

questions.stem: Once a consumer submits the six items that constitute an application, the Loan Estimate must be delivered or placed in the mail no later than:
options: Three business days after receiving the application
questions.explanation: The Loan Estimate must be delivered or mailed within three business days of receiving an application. The 'three business days before consummation' option is the Closing Disclosure rule, a frequently tested trap. Delivering at consummation is far too late, and thirty days is an ECOA notice period, not a TRID disclosure deadline.

questions.stem: The consumer must receive the Closing Disclosure no later than:
options: Within thirty days of the Loan Estimate
questions.explanation: The consumer must receive the Closing Disclosure at least three business days before consummation, allowing time to compare final terms to the Loan Estimate. Certain changes, such as an APR increase beyond tolerance, addition of a prepayment penalty, or a change in loan product, restart that three-day clock. The other options confuse this with the Loan Estimate deadline or invent timeframes.

questions.stem: For the Closing Disclosure's three-business-day rule, 'business day' counts:
options: Only Monday-Friday excluding all holidays for delivery timing under the specific (all-but-Sundays/holidays) definition
Only days the lender is open, for both LE and CD equally
questions.explanation: TRID uses a 'specific' business-day definition (all calendar days except Sundays and federal holidays) for the CD waiting period and rescission, and a 'general' definition (days the creditor is open) for other timing like LE delivery. Saturdays generally count under the specific rule.

questions.stem: A corrected Closing Disclosure and a new three-day waiting period are generally triggered when:
options: The APR becomes inaccurate beyond tolerance, a prepayment penalty is added, or the loan product changes
questions.explanation: Only three changes restart the three-business-day CD clock: an APR that exceeds the accuracy tolerance, addition of a prepayment penalty, or a change in the loan product. Most other changes require a corrected CD but no new waiting period.

questions.stem: If a required TRID disclosure contains an error affecting a fee, the creditor generally must:
options: Provide a corrected disclosure and, if a tolerance is exceeded, cure it (refund) within the required period
questions.explanation: When a disclosure error causes a tolerance violation, the creditor must correct the disclosure and cure the overcharge by refunding the excess to the borrower, generally within 60 days of consummation.

questions.stem: A valid 'changed circumstance' under TRID permits the creditor to:
options: Issue a revised Loan Estimate resetting certain fee tolerances
Increase the interest rate at will
questions.explanation: A changed circumstance (e.g., new information, a consumer-requested change, or an event beyond control affecting eligibility) allows a revised Loan Estimate that may reset the good-faith tolerance baselines for affected charges, generally within three business days of learning of the change. It is not a license to exceed tolerances arbitrarily.

questions.stem: After a valid changed circumstance, a revised Loan Estimate must generally be delivered within:
options: 3 business days of receiving information establishing the change
questions.explanation: A revised Loan Estimate reflecting a changed circumstance must generally be provided within three business days of receiving the information sufficient to establish the change, and cannot be issued on or after the Closing Disclosure is provided.

questions.stem: The Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) primarily requires lenders to:
options: Report application and loan data used to detect discriminatory lending patterns
questions.explanation: HMDA is a fair-lending law requiring covered lenders to collect and report data on applications and originations so regulators and the public can identify discriminatory patterns such as redlining and assess community credit needs.

questions.stem: The Dodd-Frank Act created which agency now responsible for most federal consumer mortgage rules?
questions.explanation: Dodd-Frank established the CFPB and transferred rulemaking and enforcement authority for many consumer financial laws (RESPA, TILA, ECOA, HMDA, and others) to it. It also created the ATR/QM framework and the LO compensation rules.
questions.primary_source_citation: Dodd-Frank Act, Pub. L. 111-203; 12 U.S.C. §5481 et seq.

questions.stem: Under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, a pre-service mortgage's interest rate during active duty is generally capped at:
questions.explanation: The SCRA caps the interest rate on obligations incurred before active duty at 6% during the period of military service, upon proper request, and provides foreclosure protections for servicemembers.

questions.stem: When a credit report contributes to a loan denial, the FCRA requires the creditor to:
options: Provide the consumer notice including the credit bureau's name and the right to a free report
Report the denial to the IRS
questions.explanation: Under the FCRA, if information in a consumer report is a basis for adverse action, the consumer must receive notice identifying the credit reporting agency and stating the right to obtain a free copy of the report and to dispute its accuracy.

questions.stem: A lender approves a borrower at a higher rate than its best customers based on the credit report. The FCRA generally requires:
options: A risk-based pricing notice (or a credit score disclosure exception notice)
questions.explanation: When a consumer receives materially less favorable terms based on a credit report, the FCRA risk-based pricing rule requires a notice, often satisfied by providing a credit score disclosure exception notice to all applicants.

questions.stem: The FACTA Disposal Rule requires businesses to:
options: Properly dispose of consumer report information to prevent unauthorized access
questions.explanation: The Disposal Rule requires reasonable measures (like shredding or wiping) to dispose of consumer report information so it cannot be reconstructed, protecting consumers from identity theft.

questions.stem: The FTC Red Flags Rule requires covered financial institutions to:
options: Provide free credit monitoring to all customers
Flag loans with high interest rates
Maintain a written Identity Theft Prevention Program
questions.explanation: The Red Flags Rule requires covered institutions and creditors to develop and implement a written Identity Theft Prevention Program to detect, prevent, and mitigate identity theft in connection with covered accounts.

questions.stem: Under BSA/AML rules, a covered mortgage lender that detects suspected mortgage fraud must:
options: File a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) and not disclose it to the subject
Tell the borrower it filed a report
questions.explanation: Covered institutions must file a SAR for suspicious transactions and are prohibited from disclosing (tipping off) the subject that a SAR was filed. This supports FinCEN's anti-money-laundering enforcement.

questions.stem: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA) requires financial institutions to:
options: Offer identical rates to all applicants
Provide privacy notices and safeguard nonpublic personal information
questions.explanation: GLBA requires financial institutions to give consumers privacy notices explaining information-sharing practices, honor opt-out rights where applicable, and maintain safeguards to protect nonpublic personal information (the Safeguards Rule).

questions.stem: An MLO cold-calls a consumer on the National Do-Not-Call Registry with no prior relationship. This is:
options: Generally prohibited without an established business relationship or consent
questions.explanation: Telemarketing to numbers on the Do-Not-Call Registry generally requires prior express consent or an established business relationship. Violations carry penalties under the TSR/TCPA framework.

questions.stem: Under the Mortgage Acts and Practices (Regulation N) advertising rule, an MLO advertisement:
options: Must include the borrower's credit score
May omit the APR entirely with no consequence
May not make material misrepresentations about loan terms
questions.explanation: Regulation N (the MAP Rule) prohibits material misrepresentations in mortgage advertising, including about rates, fees, the existence of the offer, and government affiliation. Guaranteeing universal approval is a classic prohibited misrepresentation.

questions.stem: The E-Sign Act allows electronic disclosures and signatures if:
options: The consumer never has to consent
The consumer affirmatively consents and can access the electronic records
questions.explanation: The E-Sign Act gives electronic records and signatures the same legal effect as paper, provided the consumer affirmatively consents and demonstrates the ability to access the records in the format used, after receiving specific disclosures about the arrangement.

questions.stem: The USA PATRIOT Act's Customer Identification Program requires institutions to:
options: Report all loans to the FBI
Verify the identity of customers opening accounts
questions.explanation: The Act's CIP requirements obligate financial institutions to verify the identity of persons opening accounts and to maintain records, supporting anti-terrorism and anti-money-laundering efforts.

questions.stem: Under the Homeowners Protection Act, borrower-requested cancellation of PMI is generally available when the loan balance reaches:
options: The loan is paid in full
80% of the original property value (with a good payment history)
questions.explanation: The HPA lets a borrower request PMI cancellation when the principal balance reaches 80% of the original value (with a good payment history and other conditions), and requires automatic termination at 78%. This prevents PMI from continuing indefinitely.

questions.stem: The CFPB's authority includes:
options: Writing and enforcing rules under federal consumer financial laws
questions.explanation: The CFPB writes implementing regulations for federal consumer financial laws and supervises and enforces compliance. It does not set monetary policy, approve individual loans, or license real estate agents.

questions.stem: The CFPB enforces consumer financial law primarily through:
options: Supervision, examinations, and enforcement actions against violators
questions.explanation: The CFPB supervises covered institutions, conducts examinations, and brings enforcement actions (including restitution and penalties) for violations of federal consumer financial law.

questions.stem: HUD's role in mortgage lending includes:
options: Buying loans on the secondary market
Administering FHA insurance programs and fair-housing enforcement
questions.explanation: HUD administers FHA mortgage insurance and enforces the Fair Housing Act. It wrote the original SAFE Act regulations before authority transferred to the CFPB; it does not set monetary policy or buy loans (the GSEs do).

questions.stem: A primary purpose of the SAFE Act is to:
options: Increase uniformity and consumer protection by requiring MLO licensing/registration through NMLS
questions.explanation: The SAFE Act aims to enhance consumer protection and reduce fraud by setting minimum standards for licensing and registration of mortgage loan originators and requiring participation in the NMLS. States may impose stricter standards.

questions.stem: Which document is typically filed in the public record to give notice of the lender's lien?
options: The mortgage or deed of trust
questions.explanation: The mortgage or deed of trust is recorded in the public land records to perfect and give notice of the lender's security interest. The note itself is generally not recorded.

questions.stem: A state mortgage regulator generally may NOT:
options: Exceed the authority granted by statute
questions.explanation: Regulators may license, examine, investigate, and discipline, but they may not exceed the authority the legislature delegated to them; acting beyond that authority is a common basis for challenging regulatory action.

questions.stem: The NMLS serves as:
options: The system of record for licensing and registration of MLOs across states
questions.explanation: The Nationwide Multistate Licensing System is the system of record through which MLOs are licensed/registered and through which states coordinate supervision. Consumer Access lets the public verify originators.

questions.stem: NMLS Consumer Access allows the public to:
options: Verify an MLO's license status and identifier
questions.explanation: NMLS Consumer Access is a free public website where consumers can look up an MLO or company by name or unique identifier to verify licensing status and history.

questions.stem: A state mortgage regulator's examination authority allows it to:
options: Examine a licensee's books and records and interview employees
questions.explanation: State regulators may conduct examinations, review books and records, and interview employees to assess compliance. Their authority is defined and limited by the delegating statute; they cannot exceed the powers granted by law.

questions.stem: The NMLS unique identifier assigned to an MLO:
options: Stays with the individual permanently and must appear on loan documents
Is the same as the SSN
questions.explanation: The unique identifier follows the individual across employers and states for life and must be provided on residential mortgage loan documents and advertisements so consumers can verify the originator through NMLS Consumer Access. It is not the SSN.

questions.stem: Under the LO compensation rule, an originator generally may not:
options: Receive compensation from both the consumer and another person on the same transaction
questions.explanation: The rule prohibits dual compensation, an originator receiving pay from both the consumer and another party (like the creditor) on the same transaction. Salary, per-loan, and permissible commissions are allowed.

questions.stem: Which individual must hold a state MLO license?
options: A loan processor performing only clerical tasks under supervision
A person who takes residential mortgage applications and offers or negotiates loan terms for compensation
An employee of a national bank who is a registered MLO
questions.explanation: A state MLO license is required for someone who both takes residential mortgage loan applications and offers or negotiates terms for compensation or gain. Purely clerical processors, registered (depository) MLOs, and appraisers are treated differently.

questions.stem: A state may deny an MLO license for:
options: A disqualifying criminal history or failure to demonstrate financial responsibility/character
questions.explanation: Grounds for denial include disqualifying criminal history, failure to meet financial-responsibility or character-and-fitness standards, or providing false information, not simply having debt or being new.

questions.stem: Under the SAFE Act, the minimum pre-licensing education and the minimum annual continuing education for a state-licensed MLO are:
options: 20 hours pre-licensing; 8 hours CE per year
40 hours pre-licensing; 12 hours CE per year
8 hours pre-licensing; 20 hours CE per year
questions.explanation: The SAFE Act requires a minimum of 20 hours of NMLS-approved pre-licensing education and at least 8 hours of NMLS-approved continuing education each year. States may require additional hours but not fewer, and CE is not optional for maintaining a license.

questions.stem: To renew a license, an MLO must complete at least how many hours of continuing education annually?
questions.explanation: The SAFE Act requires at least 8 hours of NMLS-approved continuing education each year, covering federal law, ethics, and nontraditional mortgage lending. CE must be completed before renewal.

questions.stem: The standard NMLS license renewal window runs:
questions.explanation: The annual NMLS renewal period runs November 1 through December 31. The MLO must have completed that year's CE and meet all standards to renew; failing to renew moves the license to a non-renewed status.

questions.stem: An MLO who lets their license lapse and later wants to originate again must generally:
options: Reinstate or reapply and meet current CE and other requirements
questions.explanation: A lapsed or inactive license generally must be reinstated (within the allowed window) or reapplied for, satisfying current CE and other standards before the MLO may originate again.

questions.stem: When a licensed MLO changes employers, they must:
options: Update their NMLS record and obtain new sponsorship
questions.explanation: A change of employer requires updating the NMLS record and obtaining sponsorship by the new employer; the license and test do not need to be redone for the move.

questions.stem: Temporary Authority to Originate (from the 2018 EGRRCPA) allows certain applicants to:
options: Originate loans for a limited period while a complete license application is pending, if eligibility conditions are met
questions.explanation: Temporary Authority lets a qualifying individual (e.g., a registered MLO moving to a state-licensed company, or a licensee moving states) originate for up to 120 days while a complete application is pending, provided conditions such as a clean history and prior licensure/registration are met.

questions.stem: A licensed MLO is authorized to:
options: Take applications and offer or negotiate residential mortgage loan terms
questions.explanation: An MLO license authorizes taking applications and offering/negotiating residential mortgage terms. Appraising, title insurance, and legal practice require separate credentials.

questions.stem: A loan processor who works under the supervision of a licensed MLO and performs only clerical support:
options: Must hold a real estate license
Must be individually licensed as an MLO
Generally does not need an MLO license for clerical/administrative tasks
questions.explanation: Clerical or support duties (assembling documents, requesting information) performed under a licensed/registered MLO's supervision generally do not require an MLO license. The line is crossed if the processor offers or negotiates terms or advises on loan terms.

questions.stem: A nondepository mortgage company that originates residential loans must:
options: Hold only a real estate license
Employ or contract licensed MLOs and hold the required company license
questions.explanation: Nondepository lenders and brokers must hold the required state company license and ensure their originators are licensed MLOs under Regulation H. Depository registration (Reg G) is a separate regime.

questions.subtopic: SAFE Act — Regulation G vs H
questions.stem: Regulation H under the SAFE Act applies to:
options: Nondepository institutions and their employees, such as state-licensed mortgage companies, brokers, and MLOs
questions.explanation: Regulation H governs state licensing of nondepository institutions and their loan originators. Regulation G covers federal registration of MLOs employed by depository institutions. The distinction between registered (depository, Reg G) and licensed (nondepository, Reg H) originators is a common Uniform State item.
questions.primary_source_citation: Regulation G, 12 CFR Part 1007; Regulation H, 12 CFR Part 1008

questions.stem: How does a felony conviction affect MLO licensing eligibility under the SAFE Act?
options: A felony in the past 7 years bars licensing; a felony involving fraud, dishonesty, breach of trust, or money laundering bars licensing permanently
questions.explanation: The SAFE Act permanently bars anyone convicted at any time of a felony involving fraud, dishonesty, breach of trust, or money laundering, and bars licensing for any felony conviction within the preceding seven years. Fingerprint-based background checks enforce these standards.

questions.stem: Before licensure, an MLO must complete at least how many hours of NMLS-approved pre-licensing education?
questions.explanation: The SAFE Act requires a minimum of 20 hours of NMLS-approved pre-licensing education, including specific hours of federal law, ethics, and nontraditional mortgage lending. States may require additional hours.

questions.stem: To satisfy the SAFE Act testing requirement, an applicant must pass the national test with a score of at least:
questions.explanation: A passing score on the SAFE MLO test is 75%. The national component with Uniform State Content satisfies both national and state knowledge requirements in participating states.
questions.primary_source_citation: 12 U.S.C. §5105; SAFE MLO Test Content Outline

questions.stem: As part of demonstrating financial responsibility, a licensed MLO must generally:
options: Be covered by a surety bond or meet a net-worth/recovery-fund alternative
questions.explanation: Financial responsibility standards require coverage by a surety bond (amount often tied to loan volume) or, where applicable, a net-worth requirement or payment into a state recovery fund. A background and credit check also inform the fitness determination.

questions.stem: Under the SAFE Act, a felony conviction affects licensing how?
options: A felony within 7 years bars licensing; a felony involving fraud/dishonesty/breach of trust/money laundering bars it permanently
questions.explanation: A felony conviction in the seven years before application bars licensure, and a felony at any time involving fraud, dishonesty, breach of trust, or money laundering is a permanent bar. Fingerprint-based background checks enforce these standards.

questions.stem: After failing the SAFE MLO test, a candidate must wait how long before the next attempt (first through third fails)?
questions.explanation: After each of the first three failures, a candidate must wait 30 days before retaking. After three consecutive failures, the wait is 180 days.
questions.primary_source_citation: NMLS Testing Handbook, test retake policy

questions.stem: An MLO's license is generally not active to originate until:
options: They are sponsored by a licensed employer in NMLS
questions.explanation: Even with an approved license, an MLO typically cannot originate until an employer sponsors them through NMLS, linking the individual license to the licensed company.

questions.stem: Under the SAFE Act, a mortgage loan originator is someone who, for compensation:
options: Takes a residential mortgage application AND offers or negotiates terms
questions.explanation: An MLO both takes a residential mortgage loan application and offers or negotiates terms of a residential mortgage loan for compensation or gain. Doing only one, or purely clerical work, generally does not meet the definition.

questions.stem: During a routine examination, a state regulator asks to review a licensee's loan files and interview staff. The licensee must:
options: Cooperate and provide access to books, records, and personnel as the law requires
questions.explanation: State mortgage regulators have statutory authority to examine a licensee's books and records and to interview employees to verify compliance. Licensees are required to cooperate; obstructing an examination is itself a violation.
questions.primary_source_citation: 12 U.S.C. §5111; State Model Law examination authority

questions.stem: An unlicensed assistant uses a licensed MLO's unique identifier to originate a loan. This is:
options: A prohibited act; each originator must use their own credentials
questions.explanation: Using another person's unique identifier or license to originate is a prohibited act. Each MLO must act under their own credentials, and allowing an unlicensed person to originate under a licensee's identifier exposes both to disciplinary action.
questions.primary_source_citation: State Model Law prohibited acts; 12 U.S.C. §5101 et seq.

questions.stem: State mortgage regulators typically require licensees to:
options: Keep records only if requested by the borrower
Retain records for a set period and produce them for examination
questions.explanation: Licensees must retain loan and business records for a period set by state law and make them available to the regulator for examination. Record retention supports supervision and enforcement of the mortgage laws.

questions.stem: A buyer wants to assume the seller's existing FHA loan. Compliant handling requires:
options: Processing the assumption per the loan's terms and the servicer's approval, including buyer qualification where required
Converting it to a new loan secretly
Letting anyone assume with no review
questions.explanation: Assumable loans (common with FHA/VA) may be taken over by a buyer, but the assumption must follow the note's terms and the servicer's process, which typically includes qualifying the assuming buyer. It cannot be done outside the lender's approval.
questions.primary_source_citation: State Model Law; FHA/VA assumption requirements

questions.stem: Which is a permissible act for a licensed MLO?
options: Using a borrower's info without authorization
Disclosing their NMLS ID and providing accurate disclosures
questions.explanation: Providing the NMLS identifier and accurate, required disclosures is permissible and expected. Unauthorized use of borrower information, steering, and unearned-fee splitting are prohibited.

questions.stem: Failure to comply with state mortgage law may result in:
options: Fines, license suspension or revocation, and other enforcement action
questions.explanation: Noncompliance can lead to civil penalties, license suspension or revocation, cease-and-desist orders, and restitution, depending on the violation and state law.

questions.stem: An MLO realizes after submission that a borrower's income was entered incorrectly. The compliant action is to:
options: Ask the borrower to match the wrong figure
Promptly correct the record and notify the underwriter of the accurate information
questions.explanation: Accuracy is a core compliance duty. On discovering an error, the MLO must promptly correct the file and convey the accurate information to the underwriter. Leaving a known error or coaching the borrower to conform to it would be a violation.
questions.primary_source_citation: State Model Law required conduct; accurate disclosure duty

questions.stem: An MLO's advertisement for residential mortgage services must include:
questions.explanation: Advertisements and loan documents must display the MLO's NMLS unique identifier so consumers can verify the originator. Advertising must also be truthful and non-misleading under applicable federal and state rules.

questions.stem: Which loan feature would disqualify a loan from Qualified Mortgage status?
options: Full verification of income and assets
Points and fees of 2.5% of the loan amount
questions.explanation: A Qualified Mortgage may not include negative amortization, interest-only payments, balloon payments (with limited exceptions), terms exceeding 30 years, or points and fees above the applicable cap (generally 3%). A 30-year term is allowed, 2.5% in points and fees is under the cap, and verifying income and assets is a requirement for a QM rather than a disqualifier.

questions.stem: A prime (non-higher-priced) qualified mortgage receives:
options: A conclusive (safe harbor) presumption of ATR compliance
questions.explanation: Prime QMs that are not higher-priced receive a conclusive presumption (safe harbor) of ATR compliance. Higher-priced QMs receive only a rebuttable presumption.

questions.stem: For a QM, points and fees generally may not exceed:
options: 3% of the loan amount (for larger loans)
questions.explanation: For a general QM on a larger loan, points and fees generally may not exceed 3% of the total loan amount, with higher percentage caps for smaller loan amounts.

questions.stem: A qualified mortgage may not have a loan term exceeding:
questions.explanation: A QM's term may not exceed 30 years. Terms beyond 30 years, along with interest-only, negative amortization, and balloon features, disqualify a loan from general QM status.

questions.stem: A conforming conventional loan is one that:
options: Meets Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac limits and underwriting guidelines
questions.explanation: A conforming loan meets the FHFA conforming loan limits and the GSEs' (Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac) underwriting guidelines, making it eligible for purchase on the secondary market. FHA loans are government-insured, and loans above the limit are jumbo.

questions.stem: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac primarily:
options: Purchase conforming loans and provide liquidity to lenders
questions.explanation: The GSEs buy conforming loans from lenders on the secondary market and securitize them, providing liquidity so lenders can originate new loans. They do not lend directly to consumers.

questions.stem: The FHFA conforming loan limit determines:
options: The largest loan the GSEs will purchase as conforming
questions.explanation: The conforming loan limit sets the maximum loan size eligible for GSE purchase as conforming; loans above it are jumbo (non-conforming). Limits are set annually and vary by area.

questions.stem: Which statement about FHA loans is correct?
options: They are available only to veterans
They require mortgage insurance (upfront plus annual) regardless of down payment
questions.explanation: FHA loans permit low down payments but require mortgage insurance, an upfront premium plus an annual premium, which on most current terms lasts the life of the loan. They are not limited to veterans (that describes VA loans), do not require 20% down, and always carry FHA mortgage insurance.
questions.primary_source_citation: National Housing Act; HUD FHA Single Family Handbook 4000.1

questions.stem: A defining feature of a VA loan is:
options: No down payment for eligible borrowers and a funding fee in place of monthly mortgage insurance
Availability to any borrower regardless of service
questions.explanation: VA loans allow eligible veterans and service members to purchase with no down payment and charge a one-time funding fee instead of monthly mortgage insurance. They are limited to those with qualifying military service and certain eligible survivors, and they do not carry monthly PMI.
questions.primary_source_citation: 38 U.S.C. Chapter 37; VA Lenders Handbook (VA Pamphlet 26-7)

questions.stem: A defining feature of an FHA loan is:
options: An upfront premium plus annual MIP regardless of down payment
questions.explanation: FHA loans permit low down payments but require mortgage insurance: an upfront premium (UFMIP) plus an annual MIP that on most current terms lasts the life of the loan. VA loans (not FHA) are the veterans' product.

questions.stem: In place of monthly mortgage insurance, a VA loan charges:
questions.explanation: VA loans do not require monthly mortgage insurance; instead they charge a one-time VA funding fee (which can be financed and may be waived for certain disabled veterans). VA loans also allow no-down-payment purchases for eligible borrowers.

questions.stem: USDA Rural Development guaranteed loans are designed for:
options: Eligible moderate-income borrowers in designated rural areas, often with no down payment
questions.explanation: USDA guaranteed loans help eligible low-to-moderate-income borrowers purchase primary residences in designated rural areas, frequently with no down payment. Income and property-location eligibility requirements apply.

questions.stem: Compared with most conventional loans, FHA and VA loans are more likely to be:
questions.explanation: Government loans (FHA/VA) are generally assumable by a qualified buyer, whereas most conventional loans contain due-on-sale clauses preventing assumption. Assumption can be attractive when rates have risen.

questions.stem: A loan whose amount exceeds the conforming loan limits set by the FHFA is called a:
questions.explanation: Loans above the FHFA conforming limits cannot be purchased by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac and are called jumbo, or non-conforming, loans. They typically carry stricter underwriting because they lack GSE backing. A bridge loan is short-term interim financing and is unrelated to loan size limits.
questions.primary_source_citation: Federal Housing Finance Agency conforming loan limit definitions (12 U.S.C. §1717)

questions.stem: Negative amortization occurs when:
options: The rate is fixed for the life of the loan
The payment is less than the interest due, so unpaid interest is added to principal
The loan is paid off early
The borrower pays extra toward principal each month
questions.explanation: Negative amortization means the periodic payment does not cover the interest owed, so the shortfall is added to the loan balance and the borrower can owe more over time than originally borrowed. It is a prohibited feature for Qualified Mortgages. The other options describe accelerated payoff, early payoff, or a fixed rate.

questions.stem: A non-qualified mortgage (non-QM) is one that:
options: Always has a lower rate than a QM
Does not meet all QM criteria (e.g., uses alternative income docs or has certain features)
questions.explanation: A non-QM loan does not satisfy all QM requirements. It may use alternative documentation or include features QMs exclude. Non-QM loans are legal but do not receive the QM presumption of ATR compliance, so lenders must still make a reasonable ability-to-repay determination.

questions.stem: An 'Alt-A' loan generally describes:
options: A loan between prime and subprime, often with reduced documentation
questions.explanation: Alt-A loans fall between prime and subprime in risk, historically featuring reduced documentation or other flexibilities for otherwise creditworthy borrowers. They are non-conforming and carry added risk.

questions.stem: A subprime loan generally serves borrowers with:
options: Weaker credit profiles, typically at higher rates to offset risk
questions.explanation: Subprime loans serve borrowers with impaired or limited credit and carry higher rates/fees reflecting greater default risk. They are non-conforming and receive extra regulatory scrutiny.

questions.stem: In a fixed-rate mortgage:
options: The principal-and-interest payment stays constant over the term
The rate adjusts with an index
questions.explanation: A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same note rate and the same principal-and-interest payment for the life of the loan, so the payment is predictable (taxes/insurance in escrow may still change). Only ARMs adjust with an index.
questions.primary_source_citation: Standard product definition; ARM disclosure contrast at 12 CFR §1026.19(b)

questions.stem: In a fully amortizing fixed-rate loan, over time each payment applies:
options: More to interest, never to principal
Increasingly more to principal and less to interest
questions.explanation: With level payments, early payments are mostly interest; as the balance declines, a growing share goes to principal. By maturity the loan is paid in full (fully amortized).

questions.stem: On an adjustable-rate mortgage, the fully indexed rate equals:
options: Start rate plus the periodic cap
questions.explanation: The fully indexed rate is the index plus the margin. The index moves with the market, while the margin is the lender's fixed add-on that remains constant for the life of the loan. Caps then limit how much the rate may actually change at each adjustment and over the loan's life.
questions.primary_source_citation: Standard ARM definition; ARM disclosure requirements at Regulation Z §1026.19(b) and §1026.20(c)

questions.stem: An ARM is quoted as '2/2/5.' The middle number represents the:
questions.explanation: In a 2/2/5 structure the first number is the initial adjustment cap, the middle number is the periodic cap limiting each subsequent adjustment, and the final number is the lifetime cap over the start rate. The margin is a separate figure and is not one of the three cap numbers.
questions.primary_source_citation: Standard ARM cap convention; consumer ARM booklet referenced in Regulation Z §1026.19(b)

questions.stem: An ARM has a start rate of 4.00%, index 3.00%, margin 2.25%, and an initial adjustment cap of 1%. What is the rate at first adjustment?
questions.explanation: Fully indexed rate = index + margin = 3.00% + 2.25% = 5.25%. The initial cap limits the increase to start + 1% = 5.00%. The new rate is the lower of the two = 5.000%.

questions.stem: An ARM has a start rate of 4.00%, index 4.50%, margin 2.25%, and an initial adjustment cap of 1%. What is the rate at first adjustment?
questions.explanation: Fully indexed rate = index + margin = 4.50% + 2.25% = 6.75%. The initial cap limits the increase to start + 1% = 5.00%. The new rate is the lower of the two = 5.000%.

questions.stem: An ARM has a start rate of 4.00%, index 3.00%, margin 2.50%, and an initial adjustment cap of 1%. What is the rate at first adjustment?
questions.explanation: Fully indexed rate = index + margin = 3.00% + 2.50% = 5.50%. The initial cap limits the increase to start + 1% = 5.00%. The new rate is the lower of the two = 5.000%.

questions.stem: An ARM has a start rate of 5.00%, index 3.50%, margin 2.25%, and an initial adjustment cap of 2%. What is the rate at first adjustment?
questions.explanation: Fully indexed rate = index + margin = 3.50% + 2.25% = 5.75%. The initial cap limits the increase to start + 2% = 7.00%. The new rate is the lower of the two = 5.750%.

questions.stem: An ARM has a start rate of 4.00%, index 3.50%, margin 2.00%, and an initial adjustment cap of 2%. What is the rate at first adjustment?
questions.explanation: Fully indexed rate = index + margin = 3.50% + 2.00% = 5.50%. The initial cap limits the increase to start + 2% = 6.00%. The new rate is the lower of the two = 5.500%.

questions.stem: In an ARM, the 'index' is:
options: A published benchmark rate the loan is tied to (e.g., SOFR)
questions.explanation: The index is an independent, published benchmark (such as SOFR) that moves with the market. Adding the fixed margin to the index yields the fully indexed rate at adjustment.

questions.stem: The margin on an ARM:
options: Is the fixed amount added to the index and stays constant for the loan's life
questions.explanation: The margin is the lender's fixed spread added to the index; it remains constant for the life of the loan while the index fluctuates.

questions.stem: A 'convertible' ARM allows the borrower to:
options: Convert the ARM to a fixed rate under stated conditions
questions.explanation: A convertible ARM gives the borrower an option to convert to a fixed-rate loan during a specified window, usually for a fee, providing a hedge against rising rates.

questions.stem: An ARM 'teaser' (initial) rate is:
options: A low introductory rate below the fully indexed rate for an initial period
questions.explanation: The teaser is a discounted introductory rate below the fully indexed rate. When it expires, the rate adjusts toward index plus margin, potentially causing payment shock, which ATR underwriting must account for.

questions.stem: A purchase-money second mortgage is:
options: A first lien used to refinance
A subordinate lien taken out at purchase, often to reduce the down payment or avoid PMI
questions.explanation: A purchase-money second mortgage is a subordinate (junior) lien originated at the time of purchase, commonly used in piggyback structures to reduce the required down payment or avoid PMI. It is repaid after the first lien in a foreclosure.

questions.stem: A balloon mortgage is characterized by:
options: Smaller periodic payments with a large lump-sum balance due at maturity
questions.explanation: A balloon loan has periodic payments that do not fully amortize the balance, leaving a large lump sum (the balloon) due at maturity. It carries refinancing/payment-shock risk and is generally excluded from standard QM status (with limited exceptions).
questions.primary_source_citation: Standard product definition; QM exclusion at 12 CFR §1026.43(e)

questions.stem: A reverse mortgage (HECM) is designed for:
options: Older homeowners (generally 62+) to convert home equity into funds with no required monthly principal-and-interest payments
questions.explanation: A HECM reverse mortgage lets eligible older homeowners (generally 62+) draw on home equity without required monthly P&I payments; the balance grows over time and is repaid when the borrower dies, sells, or moves. Counseling is required.

questions.stem: A HECM reverse mortgage generally becomes due when:
options: The borrower makes a late payment
The borrower dies, sells, or permanently moves out
questions.explanation: A HECM becomes due and payable when the last borrower dies, sells the home, or permanently moves out, or fails to meet obligations like paying taxes and insurance. There are no required monthly P&I payments during occupancy.

questions.stem: A home equity line of credit (HELOC) is best described as:
options: An open-end revolving line secured by the home, usually with a variable rate
questions.explanation: A HELOC is open-end (revolving) credit secured by the borrower's home, typically with a variable rate and a draw period followed by a repayment period. As open-end credit secured by a principal dwelling, it carries a right of rescission on applicable transactions.

questions.stem: During a HELOC's draw period, the borrower typically:
options: May borrow up to the credit limit and often pays interest-only
questions.explanation: In the draw period a HELOC borrower can advance funds up to the limit, frequently with interest-only payments; the repayment period follows, when principal and interest are amortized, often causing payment increases.

questions.stem: A construction-to-permanent loan:
options: Disburses in stages (draws) as construction progresses, then converts to permanent financing
Funds the full amount at closing regardless of progress
questions.explanation: A construction loan disburses funds in draws tied to construction milestones and often converts to a permanent mortgage on completion. During construction the borrower typically pays interest only on funds drawn.

questions.stem: During the interest-only period of an interest-only loan:
options: No principal is paid, so the balance stays level until amortization begins
questions.explanation: In the interest-only period the borrower pays only interest, so the principal balance does not decline; when the amortization period begins, payments jump (payment shock). Interest-only features disqualify a loan from QM status.
questions.primary_source_citation: Standard product definition; QM exclusion 12 CFR §1026.43(e)

questions.stem: A rate lock is:
options: A commitment guaranteeing a specified interest rate for a set period
questions.explanation: A rate lock guarantees a stated interest rate (and often points) for a defined period, protecting the borrower from rate increases before closing. If the lock expires before closing, terms may change or an extension fee may apply.

questions.stem: Table funding refers to:
options: Funding a loan from the borrower's escrow
A settlement at which the broker's loan is simultaneously assigned to the lender who supplies the funds
questions.explanation: In table funding, the loan closes in the originating broker's name but is simultaneously assigned to the lender that actually advances the funds at the settlement table. RESPA addresses disclosure in such arrangements.

questions.stem: A mortgage escrow (impound) account is used to:
options: Collect and pay property taxes and insurance
questions.explanation: An escrow account collects a portion of taxes and insurance with each payment so the servicer can pay those bills when due, spreading the cost over the year.

questions.stem: Lien priority generally determines:
options: The order in which creditors are paid in a foreclosure
questions.explanation: Lien priority (typically by recording order, 'first in time, first in right') sets the order creditors are paid from foreclosure proceeds. A first mortgage is paid before subordinate liens.

questions.stem: A borrower locks the rate but closing is delayed past the lock expiration. Typically:
options: The lock may expire, requiring re-lock at current market or an extension fee
The lender must pay the borrower
questions.explanation: A rate lock guarantees terms only for its stated period. If closing slips past expiration, the borrower may need to re-lock at prevailing rates or pay an extension fee, depending on the lender's policy.

questions.stem: When servicing of a loan is transferred, RESPA requires:
options: Notice to the borrower with a 60-day grace period for payments sent to the old servicer
questions.explanation: On a servicing transfer, the borrower must receive notice, and payments mistakenly sent to the prior servicer during a 60-day grace period cannot be treated as late. This protects borrowers during the handoff.

questions.stem: A yield spread premium historically referred to:
options: Compensation to a broker for delivering a higher-rate loan
questions.explanation: A yield spread premium was compensation paid to a broker for originating a loan at a higher rate than the borrower might otherwise qualify for. The LO compensation rule now restricts pay based on loan terms, curbing this.

questions.stem: A lender credit on the Closing Disclosure:
options: Offsets closing costs, usually in exchange for a higher interest rate
questions.explanation: A lender credit reduces the borrower's closing costs, typically in exchange for a higher interest rate (the inverse of paying points). It must be disclosed and generally cannot be reduced later.

questions.stem: Loan 'servicing' refers to:
options: Collecting payments and managing escrow, statements, and payoff
questions.explanation: Servicing is the ongoing administration of the loan after closing: collecting payments, managing escrow, sending statements, and handling payoff and default. Servicing can be sold separately from the loan.

questions.stem: On a daily simple interest loan, interest is calculated:
options: Each day on the outstanding principal balance
Once per year on the original balance
questions.explanation: Daily simple interest accrues each day on the current outstanding principal, so the timing of payments affects total interest. Paying earlier reduces accrued interest; paying later increases it, unlike a standard monthly-accrual amortization.

questions.stem: Paying discount points generally:
options: Lowers the interest rate in exchange for an upfront cost
questions.explanation: Discount points are prepaid interest paid at closing to buy down (lower) the note rate. The borrower trades an upfront cost for a lower rate and payment over time.

questions.stem: In a 2-1 temporary buydown, the interest rate is:
options: Fixed for 30 years at the buydown rate
Reduced by 2% in year one and 1% in year two, then reverts to the note rate
questions.explanation: A 2-1 buydown temporarily lowers the rate 2% below the note rate in year one and 1% below in year two, then the full note rate applies. Funds to cover the difference are typically escrowed upfront.
questions.primary_source_citation: Product structure; disclosed under Regulation Z

questions.stem: 'PITI' stands for:
questions.explanation: PITI is the full monthly housing payment: principal, interest, taxes, and insurance. It is the basis for the front-end (housing) qualifying ratio.

questions.stem: An assumable mortgage allows:
options: The lender to raise the rate at will
A qualified buyer to take over the seller's existing loan and its terms
The seller to keep the loan after selling
questions.explanation: An assumable loan lets a qualified buyer assume the seller's existing mortgage, including its rate and terms, often subject to lender approval. Many government loans (FHA/VA) are assumable; most conventional loans contain due-on-sale clauses that prevent assumption.
questions.primary_source_citation: Standard product definition; due-on-sale at 12 U.S.C. §1701j-3

questions.stem: The secondary mortgage market is where:
options: Existing loans are bought and sold among investors (e.g., the GSEs)
questions.explanation: The primary market is where lenders originate loans to borrowers; the secondary market is where those loans are bought, sold, and securitized (e.g., by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac), providing liquidity so lenders can make new loans.

questions.stem: Two loans have the same note rate, but Loan A has higher fees. Loan A's APR will be:
questions.explanation: Because the APR incorporates certain fees in addition to interest, the loan with higher fees (Loan A) will show a higher APR even at the same note rate. This helps borrowers compare true cost.

questions.stem: A subordination agreement:
options: Changes lien priority so one lien agrees to rank behind another
questions.explanation: A subordination agreement changes the normal priority so an existing lien (e.g., a HELOC) agrees to remain behind a new first mortgage, commonly used when refinancing a first lien while keeping a second.

questions.stem: A prepayment penalty charges the borrower for:
options: Refinancing with the same lender only
questions.explanation: A prepayment penalty is a fee for paying the loan off (or paying it down substantially) before a set time. QM and HOEPA rules sharply limit or prohibit prepayment penalties on covered loans.

questions.stem: The main difference between a mortgage and a deed of trust is:
options: A deed of trust involves a third-party trustee and often allows non-judicial foreclosure
One is federal, one is state
questions.explanation: A mortgage is a two-party security instrument; a deed of trust adds a neutral trustee who holds title in trust and can conduct a non-judicial foreclosure where state law permits. Both secure the note.

questions.stem: Non-judicial foreclosure generally:
options: Proceeds through a power-of-sale clause without court action, where state law allows
questions.explanation: Non-judicial foreclosure uses a power-of-sale clause (typically in a deed of trust) to foreclose without a court case, where permitted by state law; judicial foreclosure requires a lawsuit. Availability varies by state.

questions.stem: 'Conveyance' in real estate refers to:
options: The transfer of title/ownership from one party to another
questions.explanation: Conveyance is the transfer of title or an interest in real property from one party to another, typically by deed. It is central to closing a purchase transaction.

questions.stem: Which set of items constitutes an application under TRID, triggering the Loan Estimate deadline?
options: A completed appraisal and title commitment
Name, income, Social Security number, property address, estimated property value, and loan amount sought
questions.explanation: TRID defines an application by six pieces of information: name, income, Social Security number, property address, estimated property value, and the loan amount sought. Receiving all six starts the three-business-day Loan Estimate clock. A purchase contract, contact details alone, or third-party reports do not by themselves constitute an application.

questions.stem: A consumer provides the six items that make an application. This triggers the requirement to:
options: Deliver a Loan Estimate within three business days
questions.explanation: Receiving the six application items (name, income, SSN, property address, estimated value, loan amount) triggers the three-business-day Loan Estimate requirement. It does not fund the loan or waive underwriting steps.

questions.stem: On the Uniform Residential Loan Application (Form 1003), which section captures the borrower's basic identifying information, such as name and Social Security number?
questions.explanation: Section 1 collects borrower identifying and employment/income information. Section 4 covers loan and property details, Section 5 is declarations (such as bankruptcy or pending lawsuits), and Section 8 gathers demographic data for fair-lending monitoring. Knowing which URLA section holds which content is frequently tested in the origination area.
questions.primary_source_citation: Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac Uniform Residential Loan Application (Form 1003/65), Section 1

questions.stem: A borrower will use gift funds for the down payment. The MLO should:
options: Tell the borrower to call it a loan
Document the gift with a gift letter and verify the donor and transfer as program rules require
Record them as the borrower's own income
questions.explanation: Gift funds must be documented with a gift letter stating the amount, the donor, the relationship, and that no repayment is expected, plus a paper trail of the transfer as the loan program requires. Misrepresenting a gift as income or a repayable loan is fraud.

questions.stem: During application, which question is impermissible?
options: Do you plan to have children?
What is your gross monthly income?
questions.explanation: Asking about childbearing plans is prohibited under ECOA. Income, debts, and occupancy are legitimate, necessary application questions.

questions.stem: A verification of employment (VOE) is used to:
options: Confirm the borrower's stated employment and income
questions.explanation: A VOE confirms the borrower's employment status and income with the employer, supporting the income used in qualifying. It is part of documenting the borrower's ability to repay, distinct from title or rate-setting steps.
questions.primary_source_citation: Standard underwriting practice; ATR income verification 12 CFR §1026.43(c)

questions.stem: Before verifying a borrower's bank and employment records, the MLO should obtain:
questions.explanation: The borrower's signed authorization permits the lender to verify employment, income, assets, and pull credit. Verifications support the ability-to-repay determination.

questions.stem: When recommending a loan program, an MLO should:
options: Match the product to the borrower's needs and qualifications
Steer the borrower to the highest-commission product
questions.explanation: Products should be matched to the borrower's documented needs and qualifications. Recommending a costlier or riskier product to increase compensation is steering and is prohibited; suitability protects the consumer and the originator.

questions.stem: Under TRID good-faith tolerances, which charge generally falls in the 'zero tolerance' category (cannot increase from the Loan Estimate)?
options: Homeowner's insurance the borrower shops for
questions.explanation: Zero-tolerance charges (which may not increase) include fees paid to the creditor or broker, fees for services the consumer cannot shop for, and transfer taxes. Recording fees and services the borrower can shop for fall under the 10% cumulative tolerance or have no tolerance limit (like prepaid interest and insurance).

questions.stem: Charges subject to the 10% cumulative tolerance under TRID typically include:
options: Recording fees and charges for third-party services the borrower can shop for (from the creditor's list)
questions.explanation: The 10% cumulative tolerance covers recording fees and charges for third-party services the consumer is permitted to shop for when the provider is chosen from the creditor's written list. The total of these may not increase by more than 10% in good faith.

questions.stem: An application arrives missing information needed to make a credit decision. The proper action is to:
options: Wait indefinitely for the borrower to follow up
Approve conditionally and gather documents after closing
Send a notice of incompleteness stating what is needed and a reasonable deadline
Deny the loan immediately for incompleteness
questions.explanation: For an incomplete application, Regulation B provides for a notice of incompleteness that specifies the information required and sets a reasonable time to supply it, generally within the 30-day framework. An outright denial for incompleteness, indefinite inaction, or closing first and collecting later are all improper.

questions.stem: An application is incomplete. Under ECOA, the creditor should:
options: Send a notice of incompleteness stating what is needed and a reasonable time to provide it
Close the loan and gather items later
questions.explanation: For an incomplete application, Regulation B provides for a notice of incompleteness specifying the required information and a reasonable deadline (within the 30-day framework). Outright denial or inaction is improper.

questions.stem: The Loan Estimate and the special information booklet are examples of:
options: Early disclosures due shortly after application
questions.explanation: Early disclosures (Loan Estimate, special information booklet, homeownership counseling list) are provided shortly after application to inform the consumer before they commit.

questions.stem: When referring to an affiliated provider, the MLO must give the borrower:
questions.explanation: An ABA disclosure informing the borrower of the affiliate relationship and estimated charges is required, and use of the affiliate generally may not be required.

questions.stem: The interest rate and charges on a Loan Estimate that the consumer has not yet indicated intent to proceed with:
options: May expire after 10 business days if the consumer has not expressed intent to proceed
